# Summary statistics

Getting a sense of your data can be daunting, especially if you have a lot of variables.
This chapter is intended to give some quick examples of tables and plots that often
come back when exploring your data and when making reports.


## Generating some fake data

First we make a fake intervention aimed at improving fertilizer adoption.
Adoption depends on the treatment and education and a random component.
The page on [DeclareDesign](#declaredesign) has more advanced techniques
to generate fake data.

```{r}

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(modelsummary)
library(flextable)
library(estimatr)
library(ggauto)

rm(list=ls())
set.seed(1)

data <-  
  read_csv(here("data/SAFI_clean.csv"), na = "NULL") %>%
  left_join(
    {.} %>%
    select(village) %>%
    distinct(village) %>%
    mutate(
      treatment = rbinom(nrow(.),1,0.5))
  )%>%
  mutate(
    educated = rbinom(nrow(.),1,0.3),      
    u = sample(c(0.1,0.2,0.3),nrow(.),replace = TRUE),
    prob = 0.3 * treatment + 0.1 * educated + u,
    uses_fertilizer = rbinom(nrow(.),1,prob),
    treatment = factor(treatment, levels = c(0,1), labels = c("Control","Treatment")),
    uses_fertilizer = factor(uses_fertilizer, levels = c(0,1), labels = c("No Fertilizer","Fertilizer")),

  ) %>%
  select(-prob,-u) 

```





## Making a table of summary statistics

### Using modelsummary and flextable

The `modelsummary` package is the most convenient to create tables. To convert them
to word, I use the `flextable` package.

For a simple table of descriptive statistics, use the `datasummary()` function. 
I also
define a vector with variable labels, which I use throughout this chapter. Below, I use
it in the `labelizor()` function, which applies labels to a flextable object. 
I also 
apply the `autofit()` and `fix_border_issues()` functions to make the table look nicer.


```{r}

library(modelsummary)
library(flextable)

# vector for labelling variable names
labels = c(no_membrs = "# HH Members",
           years_liv = "Year in village",
           rooms = "# Rooms",
           liv_count = "# Livestock",
           no_meals = "# Meals",
           treatment = "Treated",
           educated = "Educated",
           uses_fertilizer = "Uses fertilizer",
           `(Intercept)` = "Constant")

# descriptive stats
data %>%
  select(where(is.numeric), -ends_with("ID")) %>%
  datasummary(All(.) ~ Mean + SD + min + max + Histogram , data = ., output = "flextable") %>%
  labelizor(j =1,labels = labels, part = "all")%>% 
  fix_border_issues() %>% 
  autofit()

```

Flextables can be easily exported to Word using the `save_as_docx()` function.


### Balance Table

Using `modelsummary`'s `datasummary_balance()` table function, it is easy
to create a balance table:

```{r}

treat_labels <- c("0" = "Control", "1" = "Treated")

# balance table
data %>%
  select(where(is.numeric), -ends_with("ID")) %>%
  datasummary_balance( ~ treatment , data = ., 
                      output = "flextable", stars = TRUE, 
                      dinm = TRUE, dinm_statistic = "p.value") %>%
  labelizor(j =1,labels = labels, part = "all")%>%
  labelizor(labels = treat_labels, part = "header")%>% 
  fix_border_issues() %>% 
  autofit()

```

### Advanced: Using only Flextable

For more control, the flextable package can convert data frames into good-looking tables using the 
`tabulator()` function.

First, make a data frame with summary statistics. 
I duplicate the data set using `bind_rows()` to create an overall group. 
Then I use 
[`summarize(across(...))`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/across.html)
to apply summarizing functions to a number of variables. 

```{r}

summstats <-
  bind_rows(
    data,
    data |>
      mutate(treatment = "Overall")
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    treatment = factor(
      treatment, levels = c("Control", "Treatment", "Overall")
    )
  ) |> 
  select(where(is.numeric),treatment,-key_ID) |>
  summarize(
    across(
      .cols = everything(),
      .fns = list(
        # this list defines the summary statistics to be calculated for each variable
        n =  ~sum(!is.na(.x)),
        nmiss =  \(x) sum(is.na(x)), # another way of writing an anonymous function
        mean = function (x) mean(x,na.rm=TRUE), # or like this!
        sd = ~sd(.x,na.rm=TRUE),
        min =  ~min(.x,na.rm=TRUE),
        max =  ~max(.x,na.rm=TRUE),
        iqr =  ~IQR(.x,na.rm=TRUE)
      ),
      .names =  "{.col}-{.fn}"
    ),
    .by = treatment
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -treatment,
                 names_to = c("Variable",".value"),
                 names_sep="-") 



summstats




```


Then use I flextable's `tabulator()` to make output that looks good in word. 

I've added a bunch of statistics to show the flexibility:

```{r}

library(flextable)

summstats %>%
  tabulator(
    rows = "Variable",
    columns = "treatment",
    `N` = as_paragraph(as_chunk(n - nmiss, digits=0)),
    `Mean (SD)` = as_paragraph(
      as_chunk(fmt_avg_dev(mean, sd, digit1 = 2, digit2 = 2))
    ),
    Range = as_paragraph(as_chunk(min,digits=3), "-", as_chunk(max,digits=3))) |>
  as_flextable()


```

To add a column with differences, I first define a 
[function](#functions) to compute the differences (I use a regression 
rather than a ttest, so I can cluster my standard errors etc. to this if
I need to). 
Then I use 
[`summarize(across(...))`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/across.html) 
in much the same way as above, now to create a dataframe called `difcol`. 

```{r}

library(estimatr)

get_diffs <- function(equation, clusters = NULL, weights = NULL, std.error = FALSE){

  reg <-  
    lm_robust(equation, clusters = {{ clusters }}, weights = {{ weights }}) %>% 
    broom::tidy()

  estimate <- round(reg[2,2],2)

  p <- reg[2,5]

  stars = case_when(p < 0.001 ~ "***",
                    p < 0.01 ~ "**",
                    p < 0.05 ~ "*",
                    .default = "" )

    paste0(estimate,stars)
  
}

difcol <-
  data %>%
  select(where(is.numeric),-key_ID,treatment,village) %>%
  summarize(across(.cols = c(everything(), -treatment, -village),
                   .fns = ~get_diffs(.x ~ treatment, clusters = village))) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols =everything(),
               names_to = "Variable",
               values_to="Difference")  



```

Then, all I have to do is add it to `tabulator()` using its `datasup_last` 
argument. Below, I also use a few other flextable function to make the 
table nicer. In particular, `labelizor()` to add variable
labels, for which I use the named vector I defined above.

```{r}

descriptive_table_flex <-
  summstats %>%
  tabulator(rows = "Variable",
            columns = "treatment",
            datasup_last = difcol,
            `N` = as_paragraph(as_chunk(n,digits=0)),
            `Mean (SD)` =  as_paragraph(as_chunk(fmt_avg_dev(mean, sd, digit1=2,digit2 = 2)))) %>%
  as_flextable()  %>%
  labelizor(j = "Variable", labels = labels, part = "body") %>% 
  fix_border_issues() %>% 
  autofit()

descriptive_table_flex

```

Again, to save it as a word file, use
`save_as_docx(path = "my/file.docx")`.


## Plots

### Quick plots

Can be made using `ggauto()`, which picks sensible defaults for plot type, colors etc.

Here's two factors:

```{r}
glimpse(data)

data |>
  ggauto(treatment, uses_fertilizer)

```

A factor and continuous variable:

```{r}
data |>
  ggauto(treatment, no_membrs)
  
```





maps
discrete: stacked bar charts and lollipop charts
continuous: ridge plots and ggdist
ggauto 
<!--- ggauto--->





## Plots

To make plots, use `ggplot2`. 
Plenty of help out there, here's some examples, using the following data:

```{r}
plot_data <- 
  read_csv(here("data/SAFI_clean.csv"), na = "NULL") %>%
    separate_longer_delim(items_owned, delim = ";") %>%
    mutate(value = 1) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = items_owned,
                values_from = value,
                names_glue = "owns_{items_owned}",
                values_fill = 0) %>%
    rowwise %>%
    select(-"owns_NA") %>%
    mutate(number_items = sum(c_across(starts_with("owns_"))))  
```

### Faceting {#faceting}

Faceting allows splitting a graph in multiple parts:

```{r}

plot_data %>%
    group_by(village) %>%
    summarize(across(.cols = starts_with("owns_"),
                     .fns = ~sum(.x,na.rm=TRUE) / n() * 100,
                     .names = "{str_replace(.col, 'owns_', '')}")) %>%
    pivot_longer(-village, names_to = "items", values_to = "percent") %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = village, y = percent)) +
        geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
        facet_wrap(~ items) +
        theme_bw() +
        theme(panel.grid = element_blank())


```

Note that the `.names` argument to `summarize(across())` is specified as a 
[glue string](https://glue.tidyverse.org/) that uses `str_replace()` to cut off the `"owns_"` 
bit of the column names.

For more control, look into [patchwork](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/).

### Continuous


#### Auto

`[ggauto](https://nrennie.rbind.io/ggauto/)` has a bunch of sensible defaults for plotting different types of variables.
So each section will start with that.

The default for a single variable is a raincloud plot:
```{r}

library(fabricatr)

  fabricate(
    N = 100,
    x = rnorm(N),
  ) |>
  ggauto(x)


```

Or a scatter plot for two:

```{r}

library(fabricatr)

  fabricate(
    N = 100,
    x = rnorm(N),
    y = 5 + rnorm(N)
  ) |>
  ggauto(x, y)
  



```

Or two raincloud plots for a categorical variable and a continuous variable.

```{r}
  fabricate(
    N = 100,
    cat = sample(c("a", "b"), N, replace = TRUE),
    x = rnorm(N) + (cat == "a"),
  ) |>
  ggauto(cat, x)

```


`[ggdist](https://mjskay.github.io/ggdist/index.html)` has a variety of geoms for visualizing distributions. 

The standard is the `stat_slabinterval()`, 
which is the cloud part of the raincloud plot,
combined below with `geom_weave()`, the rain drops.

Honestly, it doesn't look as good out of the box as `ggauto`, 
but it allows for a lot more flexibility. 
I also like lines:
a thin one between the 5th and 95th percentiles,
a thick one between the 25th and 75th as well as a dot at the median, 
which further helps in assessing the distribution of the data.

```{r}

library(ggdist)

fabricate(
    N = 200,
    cat = sample(c("a", "b"), N, replace = TRUE),
    x = rnorm(N) + (cat == "a")
) |>
ggplot(aes(y = cat, x = x)) +
geom_weave() +
stat_slabinterval() 
  


```

### Discrete

#### Auto 

To plot frequencies of categories, ``ggauto` uses this kind of heatmp:

```{r}

library(ggauto)
read_csv(here("data/SAFI_clean.csv"), na = "NULL") %>%
  ggauto(village, respondent_wall_type)

```


I like the type of heatmap below a bit better:

  ```{r}

read_csv(here("data/SAFI_clean.csv"), na = "NULL") %>%
  select(key_ID, village, respondent_wall_type) |>

  # put wall types in a factor, so the order makes sense
  mutate(
    respondent_wall_type = factor(
      respondent_wall_type,
      levels = c("muddaub", "sunbricks", "burntbricks", "cement")
    )
  ) |>

  # compute a column with percentage of wall type by village
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    .by = c(village, respondent_wall_type)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    pct = n / sum(n), # we will use scales::percent() later
    .by = village
  ) |> 

  # make sure the zeros are in the data
  complete(village, respondent_wall_type, fill = list(n = 0, pct = 0)) |>

  # and plot!
  ggplot(aes(y = village, x = respondent_wall_type, fill = pct)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(pct,accuracy = 1)), color = "white", size = 3) #+


```

#### Stacked bar plots

Stacked bar plots are another useful way to show distributions of categorical variables.
Here is a function that makes a stacked bar plot, with percentages on the x-axis,
counts inside the bars, and a legend at the bottom.

It uses a bunch of techniques:

- The plot is complex, but because it is contained in a reusable function,
it is easy to (re-)use.
- Category counts are computed, and added to factor labels, using `count_label()`.
- Cell counts are extracted and displayed inside the bars, using `after_stat()`.



```{r}

stacked_bar_plot <- function(df, by, fill) {
  # outputs a stacked bar chart
  
  df %>%
    # the category labels should include counts
    mutate( {{ by }} := count_label( {{ by }})) %>%
    ggplot(aes(y = {{ by }}, fill = {{ fill }})) +
    geom_bar(position = position_fill(reverse = TRUE)) +
    labs(x= "") +
    geom_text(
      stat = "count", 
      # for %: after_stat(scales::percent(count / sum(count),accuracy=1))
      aes(label = after_stat(count)), 
      position = position_fill(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE),
      color = "white"
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
    theme(legend.position="bottom") +
    guides(
      fill = guide_legend(
        nrow = 1,
        title.position="top",
        title.hjust = 0.5
      )
    )
}

count_label <- function(vector) {
  # takes a vector of strings or factor, 
  # output a factor vector with N = N included in the labels
  fct_recode(
    factor(vector), 
    !!!vector %>%
      as_tibble() %>%
      group_by(value) %>%
      summarize(n = n()) %>%
      mutate(
        value = as.character(value),
        newlabel = paste0(value,"\nn=",n)
      ) %>%
    pull(value, name = newlabel)
  )
  
}


read_csv(here("data/SAFI_clean.csv"), na = "NULL") %>%
  stacked_bar_plot(village, respondent_wall_type)


```

The point here is that plots can get quite complex, 
and by saving them in a function, you can reuse them easily.



#### Lollipop plot

A lollipop plot is a nice alternative to a bar chart.
You can make one by combining `geom_linerange()` and `geom_point()`, 
using `fct_reorder()` to put the longest lollipops are at the top. 
Here is an example, in `theme_ipsum()`, from the `hrbrthemes` package, 
which is a nice clean theme for this kind of plot.

```{r}

library(hrbrthemes)

read_csv(here("data/SAFI_clean.csv"), na = "NULL") %>%
  mutate(N = nrow(.)) %>% 
  separate_longer_delim(items_owned, delim = ";") %>%
  select(items_owned, N) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(items_owned)) %>% 
  summarize(Count = n() / first(N), .by = items_owned) %>%
  mutate(items_owned = fct_reorder(items_owned, Count)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Count, y = items_owned)) +
  geom_linerange(
    aes(y = items_owned, xmin = 0, xmax = Count),
    color = "gray"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(x = Count, y = items_owned), 
    size = 4, 
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.5),
    color = "steelblue"
  ) +
  theme_ipsum(grid = "X") + 
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot") +
  labs(
    title = "Look at this graph",
    subtitle = "People love radios, phones, and a good plough", 
    y = "Item", x = "Percent of households owning item")

```


### Maps

For maps, we use the `sf` package, and a sample data set, in geo-json format (but sf can use
all sorts of shapefiles).
I add some fake data to plot to the shapefile, 
using familiar `mutate()` syntax:

```{r}

library(sf)

file <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/johan/world.geo.json/master/countries.geo.json"


shapefile <- 
  st_read(file) %>%
  mutate(x = rnorm(n = nrow(.))) 

shapefile

```

You can then use `ggplot()` and `geom_sf()` to make a map:

You can use the `fill` aesthetic to color your shapefile:

```{r}

shapefile %>%
    ggplot(aes(fill = x)) +
        geom_sf(colour = NA) +  # removes borders
        theme_void()            # removes grid

```

You can also make an interactive map, 
which you can use in html documents created with rmarkdown,
or in shiny applications. It uses a palette I created using the `colorBin()` function.

```{r}

library(leaflet)


pallete <- colorBin(
  palette = "YlOrBr", domain = shapefile$x,
  na.color = "transparent", bins = 5
)

shapefile %>%
    #mutate(x = rnorm(n = nrow(.))) %>%
    leaflet() %>%
    addTiles() %>%
    addPolygons(fillColor = ~pallete(x),
                stroke = TRUE,
                fillOpacity = 0.9,
                color = "white",
                weight = 0.3) %>%
    addLegend(pal = pallete, values = ~x, opacity = 0.9,
              title = "Look at these pretty colours", position = "bottomleft")

```


The key to plotting this, is `geom_tile()`:

```{r}

data_for_heatmap_long |>
 ggplot(aes(y = question, x = answer, fill = pct)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(pct,accuracy = 1)), color = "white", size = 3) #+

````
